59ec699e9f:c6e8101a1e5a5e7c.title: Minimum Wages and Cost-Push Inflation: Economy-Wide Evidence from Germany
59ec699e9f:c6e8101a1e5a5e7c.author: Maximilian Priem
59ec699e9f:c6e8101a1e5a5e7c.summary: We provide the first estimates of minimum wage effects on the aggregate price level using data on the near-full German consumer basket across four national reforms, 2015-2024. Drawing on a structural model of pricing under imperfect competition, we utilise minimum wage cost shocks rather than the commonly used firm-level ‘bite’ that we show to be biased under strategic complementarity. Labour cost pass-through is 83-94 percent, at the higher end of estimates for other cost shocks. The implied macro-price elasticity is 0.024. The largest increase in October 2022 to €12 raised the aggregate price level by 0.39 percent.

59ec699e9f:2be2a6c1df388255.title: Entry Motivations Shape Preferences for Social Protection Among Platform Workers
59ec699e9f:2be2a6c1df388255.author: Thil, Laurène
59ec699e9f:2be2a6c1df388255.summary: We study platform workers' preferences for social protection â€” in the form of sick pay and paid annual leave â€” distinguishing between workers who entered platform work out of economic necessity (the "pushed") and those attracted by its flexibility and advantages (the "pulled"). Using a discrete-choice experiment administered to nearly 800 taxi, delivery, and cleaning platform workers in Germany, Italy, and Poland, we find an average willingness to pay at 3.7% of earnings for sick pay coverage and 4.6% for paid annual leave. Preferences, however, differ sharply by motivation: pushed workers are willing to forgo on average 5.3% of earnings for sick pay, and 5.6% for paid annual leave, while pulled workers' valuations are substantially lower (3.1% and 4.2%, respectively). This difference is most pronounced among workers without access to these benefits, suggesting that the absence of protections is particularly consequential for those who entered platform work under greater economic constraint. The findings indicate that the welfare impact of extending social protections to platform workers â€” as proposed by the EU Platform Work Directive â€” might depend on the share of necessity-driven workers in the platform workforce.

59ec699e9f:0d2acd1a2ef7962d.title: Consumption, Savings, and Earnings Responses to Financial Windfalls
59ec699e9f:0d2acd1a2ef7962d.author: Barry Scholnick
59ec699e9f:0d2acd1a2ef7962d.summary: We estimate the causal effects of a financial windfall on consumption, savings, and wage earnings using linked administrative data on a large sample of Canadian lottery winners. Using separate linkages of lottery winners to income tax records and credit bureau data, we estimate how lottery winnings affect consumption measured through credit card spending, savings through financial asset accumulation and debt repayment, and wage earnings from tax records. We then examine how these responses vary across the income distribution. We find that high-income individuals allocated a larger share of lottery winnings to savings and leisure, while low-income individuals spent a larger share on consumption. We illustrate the policy relevance of these heterogeneous responses through three applications: designing fiscal stimulus programs, evaluating a Universal Basic Income (UBI), and determining optimal top tax rates on wage earnings and savings.

59ec699e9f:96eceb11d490f61c.title: Adolescent Skills, Mental Health, and Early-Adult Educational and Labour-Market Outcomes
59ec699e9f:96eceb11d490f61c.author: Lindsey Macmillan
59ec699e9f:96eceb11d490f61c.summary: We examine how different dimensions of adolescent development---cognitive skills, socio-emotional functioning, and mental health---are associated with educational attainment and labour-market engagement at age 23. Using the Millennium Cohort Study, we show that these dimensions are linked to distinct outcomes in early adulthood. Attention difficulties are most strongly associated with lower educational attainment, while emotional, conduct, and peer difficulties are more closely related to weaker labour-market engagement and a higher likelihood of being not in education, employment, or training (NEET). Persistent behavioural and mental-health difficulties are particularly predictive of NEET status. We further document substantial socioeconomic inequalities in educational attainment and labour-market engagement and assess the extent to which adolescent skills and mental health account for these disparities. Our findings show that different dimensions of adolescent development are associated with distinct pathways through education and into the labour market, while also contributing to persistent socioeconomic inequalities in early-adult outcomes.

59ec699e9f:374c56dc655d6f15.title: Instrumental-Variable Estimation of Fixed-Effects Fractional-Outcome Panel Data Models, with an Application to a Major Disability Support Policy Reform
59ec699e9f:374c56dc655d6f15.author: Staub, Kevin
59ec699e9f:374c56dc655d6f15.summary: We develop a fixed-effects estimation framework for fractional-outcome panel models with a logit conditional mean. Pairwise quasi-differencing eliminates individual effects from the moment conditions, yielding a generalized method of moments estimator that is consistent under the stated moment restrictions even when the number of time period is finite and fixed. The framework allows unrestricted dependence between individual effects and covariates, accommodates endogenous regressors through instrumental variables, and extends to multivariate shares that sum to one. Boundary observations require no adjustment, and average semi-elasticities can be estimated without recovering the individual effects. We apply the framework to Australia's National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), using HILDA (Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia) survey data for 2011-2023 and instruments based on the scheme's staggered geographic rollout. We examine how NDIS receipt affects the allocation of time across paid work, housework, disability care, and remaining activities for recipients and other household members. The estimates indicate that recipients reduce work and disability care, while other household members increase disability care.

59ec699e9f:a77799a51ab463ef.title: The Introduction of Universal Child Care in New Mexico: Initial Evidence on Mothers' Labor Supply
59ec699e9f:a77799a51ab463ef.author: Herbst, Chris
59ec699e9f:a77799a51ab463ef.summary: In November 2025, New Mexico became the first U.S. state to implement a universal, no-cost child care subsidy program. This paper estimates difference-in-differences and event-study models to evaluate the impact of universal child care on mothers' short-run labor supply adjustments. Using monthly Current Population Survey data, I find that the reform produced different responses across lower- and higher-skilled mothers. For lower-skilled mothers, the policy increased employment along both the extensive and intensive margins. Conversely, higher-skilled mothers, particularly those who are married, experienced reductions in paid work, with partially offsetting increases in school enrollment. Thus, while universal child care relaxes a binding constraint among disadvantaged families, it acts as an in-kind transfer for their advantaged counterparts.

59ec699e9f:b09a42580ba445b8.title: Capital-Skill Complementarity Beyond Firm Boundaries
59ec699e9f:b09a42580ba445b8.author: Stijn Vanormelingen
59ec699e9f:b09a42580ba445b8.summary: New machinery has long been argued to raise the relative demand for skilled labor, yet firm-level evidence finds no such shift at investing firms. We resolve this puzzle by looking beyond firm boundaries. Linking Belgian data on capital investments, buyer–supplier transactions, and worker skills, we show that the skill bias of new machinery arises entirely at external suppliers. Following machinery investment spikes, purchases from suppliers raise firms’ total demand for high-STEM workers by 45%, three times the rise for other skill groups, while in-house hiring raises it by less than 5%, evenly across skill groups. This external demand comes first from machine integrators and later from complementary services such as software, and is stronger for smaller firms, lumpier investments, and rapidly advancing capital, consistent with fixed and adjustment costs of hiring high-STEM workers in-house. In a general-equilibrium model estimated on our event studies, the rise in machinery per worker from 2003 to 2021 raises relative demand for high-STEM workers by 8.8 log points and their wage premium by 3.1. Measured on payrolls alone, both would fall.

59ec699e9f:d4c2ef32d1497188.title: Labor Supply and Wages over the Life Cycle: Human Capital and Disability Benefits
59ec699e9f:d4c2ef32d1497188.author: Tom Waters
59ec699e9f:d4c2ef32d1497188.summary: Work experience has been found to be a key determinant of work and wages for educated women, but it seems to play a smaller role for the less educated. For them, welfare, tax credits and family composition matter more, and increasingly so does participation in disability programmes. Here we document how labor supply, wages, health, and disability claims have evolved in the UK over the last three decades, and examine how reforms to tax credits, disability benefits and other welfare programs have changed work incentives over this period. We then introduce these features into an empirical dynamic structural model of life-cycle labor supply, human capital and disability benefit application, in which human capital combines health capital, experience accumulated in work, and education. Estimating the model on a panel of working-age women in the UK, we examine the interactions between experience capital and health capital in driving life-cycle earnings across different education groups. Our results highlight the importance of interactions in the disability benefit, welfare and tax-credit systems for understanding the life cycle pattern of hours, employment, earnings, and disability claims, and for evaluating policy counterfactuals.

59ec699e9f:dec6e54e4738e321.title: Physicians' Occupational Licensing and the Quantity-Quality Trade-off
59ec699e9f:dec6e54e4738e321.author: Cristóbal Otero
59ec699e9f:dec6e54e4738e321.summary: Occupational licensing is a widespread quality regulation that potentially increases the quality of labor but reduces its quantity. We provide a theoretical framework to empirically quantify this trade-off in public hospitals, where both clinical quality and physician shortages are critical concerns. Using quasi-exogenous variation driven by a recent and unprecedented migration of physicians to Chile, together with growth in domestic medical schools, we show that more physicians improve patient outcomes, while lower-quality physicians—as measured by licensing exam performance—worsen them. Incorporating these findings into our theoretical framework, we evaluate the implications of locally changing the stringency of the licensing policy.

59ec699e9f:e18367ee31a0e58b.title: How Heavily Are PhD Students Offloading Their Scientific Writing to AI? Evidence from US STEM PhD Dissertations
59ec699e9f:e18367ee31a0e58b.author: Hansen Zhang
59ec699e9f:e18367ee31a0e58b.summary: Large language models are diffusing rapidly into science, raising concerns that delegating research writing to AI may undermine the development of expertise that scientific training is supposed to build. We measure AI-generated writing in the dissertations of a near-census of US STEM PhD graduates from 2019 to 2026 and link graduates to their subsequent employment. AI writing is absent before 2023, present in 29% of dissertations filed in 2026, and rapidly growing. Use is more common among students from non-English-speaking countries and at lower-ranked programs. Among graduates in the same program and cohort, those whose dissertations contain AI writing are less likely to enter academic research careers and more likely to enter non-tenure-track roles or industry, with this pattern strongest among US-origin students. At the same time as AI may increase research productivity, it thus appears to also be displacing a potentially important portion of the work through which scientific expertise is developed.

59ec699e9f:c5b030775cec6849.title: Consumption, Savings, and Earnings Responses to Financial Windfalls
59ec699e9f:c5b030775cec6849.author: Barry Scholnick
59ec699e9f:c5b030775cec6849.summary: We estimate the causal effects of a financial windfall on consumption, savings, and wage earnings using linked administrative data on a large sample of Canadian lottery winners. Using separate linkages of lottery winners to income tax records and credit bureau data, we estimate how lottery winnings affect consumption measured through credit card spending, savings through financial asset accumulation and debt repayment, and wage earnings from tax records. We then examine how these responses vary across the income distribution. We find that high-income individuals allocated a larger share of lottery winnings to savings and leisure, while low-income individuals spent a larger share on consumption. We illustrate the policy relevance of these heterogeneous responses through three applications: designing fiscal stimulus programs, evaluating a Universal Basic Income (UBI), and determining optimal top tax rates on wage earnings and savings.

59ec699e9f:5e726b4adc7b0fe8.title: Workers, Firms, and Spatial Wage Inequality: Evidence from Hungarian Local Labor Markets
59ec699e9f:5e726b4adc7b0fe8.author: László Czaller
59ec699e9f:5e726b4adc7b0fe8.summary: This paper examines how workers and employers jointly shape spatial wage disparities across Hungarian local labor markets. We combine longitudinal linked employer–employee administrative data for 2012–2022 with functional local labor markets constructed from district-to-district commuting flows in the 2022 Hungarian Census. Our preferred delineation contains 29 commuting zones and raises the share of employed residents working within the same unit above 90 percent, compared with 72 percent for districts and 81 percent for counties. We estimate an additive worker–employer fixed-effect wage model and decompose wage variation at the individual level, between commuting zones, and within commuting zones. Differences in commuting-zone mean wages account for 2.8 percent of national log-wage variance and 1.1 percent when the Budapest commuting zone is excluded. Although the between-zone component is modest, its structure is systematic: zones with higher average worker effects also tend to have higher average employer wage premia, so the spatial alignment of worker and employer components accounts for an important part of spatial wage differences. Wage dispersion and the relative importance of worker heterogeneity, employer premia, and worker–employer sorting within local labor markets also vary substantially across the country. The results indicate that spatial wage disparities in Hungary reflect not only differences in workers’ earnings potential and the employer premia attached to their jobs, but also how these components are combined across local labor markets.

59ec699e9f:a447ce1c46303d0e.title: Which Workers Left the Labor Force Post-COVID Recession and Why?: Filing, Tax Credit Take-Up, and Labor Force Engagement by Occupation
59ec699e9f:a447ce1c46303d0e.author: Michael Stevens
59ec699e9f:a447ce1c46303d0e.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic caused a sharp initial rise in unemployment, followed by an unexpectedly tight labor market. Using a panel of tax data containing newly assembled information on worker occupation, we document persistent labor force exit, especially among low-income and low-skill workers. Low-skilled unmarried men are by far the most likely to exit, reinforcing recent concerns regarding the economic and social engagement of this group. Contrary to prevailing theories, we find little evidence that school closures, virus exposure, stimulus payments, or unemployment benefits explain these exits. Nor is the exit explained by additional upgrading of occupations or firm quality. Individuals who leave the labor force do not (on average) make up the missing income; however, self-employment income replaces roughly a quarter of the lost W-2 income. The facts suggest that the willingness to work for low pay decreased and preferences for leisure and job flexibility increased among a large set of workers who have found ways to get by with less income. These results have implications for tax policy, fiscal projections, and labor market dynamics in the post-pandemic economy.

59ec699e9f:0a01c3a05b0d2cb2.title: Gang Crackdowns
59ec699e9f:0a01c3a05b0d2cb2.author: María Micaela Sviatschi
59ec699e9f:0a01c3a05b0d2cb2.summary: What are the consequences of restoring state authority in territories governed by criminal organizations? Combining household surveys and administrative records with detailed maps of former gang-controlled areas, we study how El Salvador’s 2022 State of Exception, which ended two decades of gang territorial control, reshaped Salvadoran society. We find that the removal of gang control integrated previously segmented labor markets, improving mobility, employment outcomes, household income, and financial inclusion. Areas with greater pre-2022 gang exposure also experienced larger increases in business formation and property investment. However, the legacy of criminal governance persists through residence-based discrimination: employers remain less willing to hire otherwise identical applicants from former gang-controlled neighborhoods. Finally, although overall support for the crackdowns remains high, individuals who witnessed police abuse report substantially greater distrust of the police and the national government, suggesting that abuses of state authority may undermine the political sustainability of tough-on-crime policies.

59ec699e9f:876437d22495089d.title: Avoiding Regulation: Evidence from Nursing Homes
59ec699e9f:876437d22495089d.author: Riley League
59ec699e9f:876437d22495089d.summary: We study strategic responses by firms to threshold-based regulations. We document extensive bunching in response to additional staffing requirements for California nursing homes with at least 100 beds. To estimate the regulation’s effect on staffing, we develop a novel treatment effects estimator for threshold-based regulations under precise manipulation, by decomposing firms into response types based on counterfactual and realized staffing and size, separating causal effects from selection. We estimate that higher staffing above the threshold is nearly entirely due to selection, with low-staffing facilities manipulating their size to avoid the regulation. These size distortions limit access, particularly for disadvantaged patients.

59ec699e9f:36f08e7f123cb64b.title: Schooling and Political Activism in the Early Civil Rights Era
59ec699e9f:36f08e7f123cb64b.author: Bhashkar Mazumder
59ec699e9f:36f08e7f123cb64b.summary: Does education lead to political activity? We find that a large, early 20th century school construction program, the Rosenwald schools, led to more NAACP branches in the rural South starting in the early 1940s, i.e. prior to the classic U.S. Civil Rights Movement. Branch growth was stronger where Jim Crow occupational segregation prevented Black men from realizing some of the economic gains of their education. Our findings lend support to theories emphasizing that economic context can act as a critical mediator in determining whether human capital causes political engagement.

59ec699e9f:f6618a5a531cd251.title: Asymmetric Information in Wage Contracts: Experimental Evidence and Welfare Implications
59ec699e9f:f6618a5a531cd251.author: Daniel Herbst
59ec699e9f:f6618a5a531cd251.summary: Compared to self-employment or performance-based pay, fixed wages reduce earnings uncertainty but are prone to market distortions through moral hazard and adverse selection. Using a model of wage contracts under asymmetric information, I show that these distortions map to marginal treatment response functions in a marginal treatment effects (MTE) framework. I apply this framework to a field experiment in which data-entry workers choose between a randomized fixed wage and a piece rate. I find evidence of both moral hazard and adverse selection: Fixed wages reduce worker productivity by an estimated 8.74 percent relative to the mean. Meanwhile, a 10 percent increase in the wage offer attracts a marginal worker whose productivity is higher by 1.90 percent of the mean. Using semi-parametric MTE estimation, I calculate the welfare loss associated with asymmetric information and the marginal values of public funds (MVPFs) for policies aimed at recovering this loss. I find that a tax on piece rates can mitigate adverse selection into fixed wages, generating tax revenue at social costs as low as $0.88 per dollar.

59ec699e9f:d6a700b3dd4eeed9.title: High and Rising Institutional Concentration of Award-Winning Economists
59ec699e9f:d6a700b3dd4eeed9.author: Hanzhang Zhou
59ec699e9f:d6a700b3dd4eeed9.summary: We analyze the academic affiliations of nearly 6, 000 award-winning researchers in 18 major fields in the natural sciences, engineering, and social sciences from the 1820s to the 2020s, focusing on the 1960s onward. The analysis reveals a trend of declining concentration in the institutional affiliations of award-winning researchers, shifting from a few science-strong universities in high-income countries to a more diverse set of institutions across the world. The decline in concentration is observed in all fields except one: economics. The institutional affiliations of prizewinning economists have become more concentrated over time, making economics the most concentrated field. We associate the higher concentration of prizewinning work in economics with the field’s stronger sorting by institutional prestige, its lower reliance on specialized equipment and instruments, and its assessment of findings based on a synthesis of evidence rather than on decisive experiments or proofs. We discuss the benefits and costs of this high and rising institutional concentration of prizewinning economists.

59ec699e9f:7fb14afce539e12b.title: Digital Social Pressure, Managerial Decision-Making and Worker Performance: Evidence from Professional Football
59ec699e9f:7fb14afce539e12b.author: James Reade
59ec699e9f:7fb14afce539e12b.summary: Digital platforms expose workers and managers to immediate, public, and persistent evaluations from external audiences, creating a form of social pressure that may shape workplace decisions. We examine whether such digital social pressure predicts subsequent opportunity allocation and worker performance, using professional football as a high-frequency empirical setting. We link player-match data from Europeâ€™s five major leagues to post-match Twitter commentary and construct measures of negative sentiment, toxicity, and racial abuse. Comparing players with themselves over time and teammates in the same current match, we find that greater negative sentiment is associated with a lower probability of appearing in the teamâ€™s next match. Toxicity shows a similar but less stable association, while racial-abuse intensity is imprecisely estimated when the measures enter jointly. By contrast, associations with performance conditional on a subsequent appearance are small and imprecise. Overall, the findings suggest that digital social pressure is reflected more strongly in the allocation of subsequent opportunities than in worker performance, showing how public evaluations generated outside formal organizational boundaries can become part of the reputational environment surrounding internal managerial decisions.

59ec699e9f:d7ac4d46dd478bfe.title: Seniority rules and selection into job loss
59ec699e9f:d7ac4d46dd478bfe.author: Häggkvist, Martin
59ec699e9f:d7ac4d46dd478bfe.summary: How much are employers willing to pay to sidestep employment protection? I study this in the context of seniority rules, aiming to shield tenured workers from job loss. Using detailed and unique Swedish layoff notification data matched with administrative registers, I identify the set of workers at risk of dismissal and construct counterfactual displacement lists based on the mandated layoff order. I find that workplaces with relatively more productive junior workers are significantly less likely to follow the seniority order. A one-standard-deviation increase in the relative productivity of recent hires reduces compliance by 7.7 percentage points. To circumvent the default order, employers provide higher severance pay and longer advance notice to senior workers, indicating that firms pay for the right to retain more productive workers. These results indicate that seniority rules impose efficiency costs on employers as employment protection is traded for financial compensation.

59ec699e9f:256b087b76b355e6.title: The Recent Evolution of AI-Related Labor Demand
59ec699e9f:256b087b76b355e6.author: Kevin Rinz
59ec699e9f:256b087b76b355e6.summary: AI mentions in US job advertisements have increased substantially since the beginning of 2024. The increase is concentrated in occupations more intensely exposed to the capabilities of large language models: one additional standard deviation of exposure is associated with a 3.1 percentage point increase in the rate at which job ads mention AI. Alongside this increase in AI mentions, more exposed occupations have seen job postings stabilize after a period of relative decline, posted wages rise, and hires and separations rise, all relative to less exposed occupations. Realized wages for new hires have risen consistent with posted wages, while wages of continuously employed workers have declined, possibly because exposed occupations have seen labor markets become less tight.

59ec699e9f:6304be0cb15558aa.title: Human Capital Accumulation Across Space
59ec699e9f:6304be0cb15558aa.author: Esteban Rossi-Hansberg
59ec699e9f:6304be0cb15558aa.summary: This paper studies how human capital shapes the economic geography of development. We propose a model in which human capital acquisition costs vary across space, and regions with higher human capital invest more in human-capital-augmenting technology. Locations are interconnected through costly migration and trade. Using data on local income and schooling, we quantify the model at a 1° x 1° resolution globally. Over two centuries, the model mostly predicts persistence in the spatial distribution of development. Proportionally lowering education costs in sub-Saharan Africa raises local outcomes but lowers global welfare, while the same policy in Latin America improves global welfare. An alternative policy that equalizes educational costs across sub-Saharan Africa generates worse outcomes, as population shifts within the region toward less productive areas. These results are driven by the estimated negative correlation between education costs and local fundamentals, as well as spatial inefficiencies due to externalities.

59ec699e9f:c589c429fb1ca891.title: Assessing Financial Preparedness in Old Age in Asia: Evidence from the Republic of Korea
59ec699e9f:c589c429fb1ca891.author: Donghyun Park
59ec699e9f:c589c429fb1ca891.summary: We estimate expected financial resources in old age—including public transfers, family transfers, accumulated assets, and post-retirement labor income—and compare them with target consumption needs. The sample is divided into a reference group (individuals at or beyond retirement age) and a target group (pre-retirement individuals). Two retirement scenarios are considered: (i) a statutory retirement age of 62 for both men and women, and (ii) effective retirement ages of 66 for men and 65 for women. Results are presented by gender and place of residence. We find substantial heterogeneity in financial preparedness, with women facing significantly larger shortfalls than men. Continued work and family transfers remain critical pillars of old-age support, highlighting the transitional nature of the Republic of Korea’s welfare regime.

59ec699e9f:001fd3f07fce3e37.title: Applying but not Receiving: Longer Working Lives and Institutionalized Health Investment
59ec699e9f:001fd3f07fce3e37.author: Felix Weinhardt
59ec699e9f:001fd3f07fce3e37.summary: Rising life expectancy and demographic change have increased the share of older workers, making their health and productivity central to aging societies. We study whether longer working lives translate into investments in work-related health before retirement. Exploiting a pension reform in Germany in a Regression Discontinuity Design, we show that women facing longer careers are more likely to apply for work-related rehabilitation, particularly those in poorer health or with weaker labor market attachment. Despite higher application and approval rates, this demand does not translate into higher rehabilitation completion. Together with intermediate outcomes, our findings are most consistent with capacity constraints in program delivery.

59ec699e9f:2c2f4f2e8a78ab2b.title: Educating like China
59ec699e9f:2c2f4f2e8a78ab2b.author: Yuan Zi
59ec699e9f:2c2f4f2e8a78ab2b.summary: This paper shows that human capital accumulation can accelerate structural transformation without accelerating growth. We study China's 1999 higher education expansion, a large, rapid, and largely unanticipated increase in college graduates. We find that more exposed prefectures experienced larger increases in the skilled-labor share and shifted employment and value added from agriculture toward services. The reallocation extended to low-skilled workers. Consumer services absorbed most of the increase in employment, while producer services accounted for a disproportionate share of high-skilled employment growth. Yet more-exposed prefectures did not grow faster. A four-sector model rationalizes these patterns, showing how greater skill supply can generate broad-based servitization, but also a Baumol-type growth penalty when labor reallocates toward slower-growing sectors. Our findings highlight that the payoff to higher education depends not only on how much skill it creates, but also on whether the resulting structural transformation directs resources toward the economy's engines of productivity growth.

59ec699e9f:6ab7732edcb540ec.title: Vacancy referrals and broader job search: the role of spillovers among caseworkers
59ec699e9f:6ab7732edcb540ec.author: Hossain, Mohammad Zariab
59ec699e9f:6ab7732edcb540ec.summary: This paper provides the first causal evidence of behavioral spillovers in public employment services (PES). Using rich Swedish administrative data from 2004–2018 and a difference-in-differences design exploiting caseworker moves across local PES offices, I show that caseworker’s broader vacancy referral behavior—vacancy referrals outside a job seeker’s stated preferences—responds strongly to the local work-practice styles. I also examine how these practice-environment shocks of the movers (caseworkers) affect their job seekers. Taken together, the evidence suggests that local referral practices and the surrounding organizational environment play an important role in shaping caseworker behavior, with consequences for job seekers’ reemployment prospects.

59ec699e9f:4239734b7ce55501.title: Better Technology, Worse Motivation: Generative Artificial Intelligence’s Mediocrity Trap
59ec699e9f:4239734b7ce55501.author: Zibo Zhao
59ec699e9f:4239734b7ce55501.summary: While generative artificial intelligence (AI) promises productive efficiency, it can paradoxically lead to lower quality work. We conducted an experiment with professional illustrators and found that AI assistance flattens the quality curve—it accelerates initial gains but sharply diminishes the returns on sustained effort. Faced with this, a significant number of professionals made a strategic choice: they sacrificed the final quality to save time. Our finding highlights a critical challenge for generative AI, which can weaken the motivation required for creative excellence and innovation. In developing economies, where governments may seek to boost growth by using generative AI to substitute for scarce skills, our results suggest that such gains may come at the cost of the sustained effort through which higher-quality work and expertise are built.

59ec699e9f:8f373fc12a89bb60.title: Assessing the macroeconomic and fiscal effects of non-communicable diseases
59ec699e9f:8f373fc12a89bb60.author: OECD
59ec699e9f:8f373fc12a89bb60.summary: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) impose substantial costs on economies by reducing workforce participation and productivity, increasing healthcare expenditure and affecting public finances. Quantifying these costs helps policymakers assess the potential economic and fiscal gains from public health policies that reduce the burden of NCDs. The OECD has developed a framework [O1.1] that combines its OECD SPHeP NCDs microsimulation model, which projects the effects of NCDs on population health, labour market outcomes and healthcare expenditure, with the OECD long-term growth model. Previously, the framework estimated the burden of NCDs on GDP through their effects on workforce participation and productivity. This paper extends the framework by adding healthcare expenditure as a second channel through which NCDs affect GDP, capturing how resources used to treat NCDs could otherwise support investment and capital accumulation in the economy. It also broadens the analysis to assess how NCDs affect public expenditure, including healthcare, pensions and other age-related spending. Applied to four major NCDs across 49 OECD, EU and G20 countries, the enhanced framework provides a more comprehensive assessment of their burden on GDP and public finances.

59ec699e9f:21b16bac984c5676.title: Distributional Intersectional Fairness in AI-Supported Job Matching: Evidence on Amplification, Trade-Offs, and Residual Risk
59ec699e9f:21b16bac984c5676.author: Weber, Enzo
59ec699e9f:21b16bac984c5676.summary: "Despite widespread recognition of intersectionality in discrimination research, most algorithmic fairness evaluations remain limited to single-attribute group comparisons or individual-level prediction errors. This paper introduces a distributional approach to intersectional fairness that evaluates how machine learning models reshape the allocation of outcomes across intersecting social groups. Using large-scale administrative labour-market data from public employment services, we analyse an AI-supported job matching system with 141 occupational classes and more than three million observations. We measure intersectional disparities via Jensen–Shannon divergence and compare observed occupational distributions to model-implied allocations. We show that unconstrained models do not merely reproduce existing labour-market structures but systematically amplify intersectional disparities across occupations. Fairness-aware regularization reduces aggregate disparities but introduces a pronounced trade-off with predictive performance and reallocates distortions across occupations rather than eliminating them. Counterfactual averaging achieves substantial reductions in occupation-level disparities while preserving most predictive performance, may provide a more favourable fairness-performance trade-off in this application setting than directly constraining model outcomes. To identify localized fairness risks, we propose an occupation-level audit mechanism that flags cases with unusually large distributional shifts. Even under strong fairness constraints, a small number of occupations exhibit substantial residual distortions, indicating that fairness interventions compress rather than remove inequality. Our results demonstrate that fairness in large-scale decision-support systems must be evaluated at the level of outcome distributions. More broadly, they highlight the limits of purely technical mitigation and the need to combine fairness-aware modelling with explainability,…

59ec699e9f:bf5f9e89b5af404f.title: The Early Spatial Diffusion of Generative AI in Japan: Retrospective Adoption Cohorts, Composition versus Place, and the Role of Aging and Labor Shortages
59ec699e9f:bf5f9e89b5af404f.author: Takahiro Tabuchi
59ec699e9f:bf5f9e89b5af404f.summary: Japan has the lowest rate of generative AI use among major economies, yet little is known about how the technology has spread within the country. This study uses the sixth wave of the Japan COVID-19 and Society Internet Survey (JACSIS, N = 27, 630), which asks respondents when they first started using generative AI, to reconstruct cumulative adoption curves for Japanese municipalities from November 2022 to January 2026. Because every respondent became able to adopt at the same moment, the release of ChatGPT, the retrospective cohorts support a discrete-time hazard analysis without left truncation. Linking postal codes to municipal statistics, we document four findings. First, adoption follows the urban hierarchy: by January 2026, 50% of residents of the quintile of municipalities with the highest population density had adopted, compared with 35% in the quintile with the lowest population density, and the ratio between the two rose from 0.55 to 0.71 over the four periods, indicating relative convergence alongside a widening absolute gap. Second, most of the geographic gradient reflects who lives where rather than where they live: individual characteristics explain 64% of the population-density coefficient, and the coefficients on population density and on distance to Tokyo become statistically indistinguishable from zero once individual controls are included. Third, municipal population aging is negatively associated with adoption beyond its compositional effect, but only in the first two years of diffusion. Fourth, the job openings-to-applicants ratio in the respondent's workplace area is positively associated with work-related adoption and unrelated to purely private adoption, a pattern consistent with labor scarcity pulling generative AI into workplaces. The association is statistically significant but economically small: a one-point increase in the ratio is associated with a work-adoption probability less than one percentage point higher. Regional differences…

59ec699e9f:c5a3d1516354aed9.title: The Supply-Side Effect of Immigration on Prices: Evidence from Nursing Homes
59ec699e9f:c5a3d1516354aed9.author: Izabela Wnuk-Soares
59ec699e9f:c5a3d1516354aed9.summary: We study how immigration affects prices through changes in labor supply. Using policy-driven increases in immigration to Germany and administrative data covering the universe of nursing homes, we find that one additional foreign-born woman per 100 residents reduces nursing-home care prices by 2.6 percent. The price effects are concentrated in more competitive markets. Examining potential mechanisms, we find that immigration lowers labor costs as nursing homes shift toward lower-paid foreign-born workers. We find no evidence of declines in inspection-based measures of quality or of scale effects. Finally, immigration increases the use of informal care, potentially strengthening competitive pressure from the broader care market.

59ec699e9f:632f8fe0b49f909f.title: Relaxing Immigration Restrictions in a Peripheral Region: Evidence from Finnish North Karelia
59ec699e9f:632f8fe0b49f909f.author: Jeremias Nieminen
59ec699e9f:632f8fe0b49f909f.summary: Several countries use immigration liberalization as a place-based policy tool, but evidence on its regional effects remains almost entirely descriptive. We examine the causal impact of removing labor market testing (LMT) regulations for labor immigrants in all occupations in the remote Finnish region of North Karelia. The reform allowed firms to hire non-EU foreign workers in all occupations without first advertising jobs to domestic applicants, resulting in a 14% rise in the stock of immigrant workers. Using synthetic control and difference-in-differences methods, we estimate causal effects of the reform at the regional, municipal, firm establishment, and individual levels. The reform caused immigrant inflows to increase primarily in cities and in specific types of occupations, i.e., low-paying occupations and ISCO groups 5, 7, 8, and 9. Across the firm size distribution, the increases concentrate around the median and the top. We find little evidence that the policy had meaningful effects on other regional or municipal outcomes: immigration liberalization boosted labor supply without generating transformative medium-term regional effects.

59ec699e9f:64318c7266598712.title: Competing for workers: labor market transmission of firm export
59ec699e9f:64318c7266598712.author: Gorshkov, Andrei
59ec699e9f:64318c7266598712.summary: We study the transmission of firm-specific export shocks through labor markets, examining how these shocks influence workers’ wages at competing firms via labor market competition. Using rich Danish administrative data, a flexible, empirically driven definition of workers’ outside options, and an identification strategy based on world import demand shocks, we show that both own-firm and competitor export shocks raise incumbent workers’ wages. These export-driven shocks also trigger competitive worker reallocation, as expanding exporters poach workers from other firms. The results indicate spillover effects of export shocks extending to non-exporting firms.

59ec699e9f:d0601d6bb1f0c78d.title: Minimum Wage Reform in a Wartime Economy : Simulating Impacts from Ukraine’s Proposed Reform
59ec699e9f:d0601d6bb1f0c78d.author: Moessinger, Martin
59ec699e9f:d0601d6bb1f0c78d.summary: While the literature on the minimum wage is largely retrospective, analyzing impacts of past policy changes, this paper is uniquely forward-looking, forecasting how a proposed reform in Ukraine would affect future employment, earnings, and social contributions. The analysis simulates these effects by mimicking a proposal that would set a minimum wage floor equal to 40 percent of the previous year’s average wage once martial law is over and increasing the minimum wage by two percentage points annually until reaching 50 percent of the previous year’s average wage. The analysis draws on a 10 percent random sample of 2023 worker-level data from the Pension Fund of Ukraine, covering all jobs with pension contributions in the private sector and nonmilitary public sector. The results indicate that, under the proposal, by the end of the five-year transition period, the minimum wage would be 45 percent above the level it would have reached if adjusted only for wage inflation, which serves as the counterfactual. Projected job losses would be modest (0.51–1.03 percent), while total earnings would increase by up to 3.24 percent. The effect on social contributions and taxes would be the same as the effect on earnings since they are a fixed percentage of earnings in Ukraine. Applied to an administrative data set covering all formal sector workers, the methodology developed in the paper offers a useful tool for policy makers to anticipate the likely effects of the minimum wage reforms that are being considered. The paper concludes by discussing policy implications.

4a32a2255e:6b44000d8f244708.title: Unpacking place transformation
4a32a2255e:6b44000d8f244708.author: OECD
4a32a2255e:6b44000d8f244708.summary: Many communities across the OECD are struggling to keep pace with economic change. Persistent disparities in employment rates, skills mismatches and economic inactivity reflect a fractured geography of opportunities, and long-lasting effects of economic shocks and structural change. The consequences are not just economic, but also deeply personal, with potential to fuel disillusionment and to reinforce cycles of disadvantage. Yet, successful examples of transformation highlight that decline is not inevitable. Experiences from success stories can inform how to both better address scars from the past as well as more proactively adapt to future transitions. This paper provides a fresh perspective on place transformation, in particular one that better reflects the role of “soft infrastructure” like local leadership and place identity, bridges local and external drivers of change, and better integrates economic and social outcomes.

4a32a2255e:6ed835f06f6a9429.title: Relaxing Immigration Restrictions in a Peripheral Region: Evidence from Finnish North Karelia
4a32a2255e:6ed835f06f6a9429.author: Jeremias Nieminen
4a32a2255e:6ed835f06f6a9429.summary: Several countries use immigration liberalization as a place-based policy tool, but evidence on its regional effects remains almost entirely descriptive. We examine the causal impact of removing labor market testing (LMT) regulations for labor immigrants in all occupations in the remote Finnish region of North Karelia. The reform allowed firms to hire non-EU foreign workers in all occupations without first advertising jobs to domestic applicants, resulting in a 14% rise in the stock of immigrant workers. Using synthetic control and difference-in-differences methods, we estimate causal effects of the reform at the regional, municipal, firm establishment, and individual levels. The reform caused immigrant inflows to increase primarily in cities and in specific types of occupations, i.e., low-paying occupations and ISCO groups 5, 7, 8, and 9. Across the firm size distribution, the increases concentrate around the median and the top. We find little evidence that the policy had meaningful effects on other regional or municipal outcomes: immigration liberalization boosted labor supply without generating transformative medium-term regional effects.

4a32a2255e:1077669d0ec7db22.title: Playing Europe's hand: competitiveness, place and the high stakes of territorial myopia
4a32a2255e:1077669d0ec7db22.author: Dijkstra, Lewis
4a32a2255e:1077669d0ec7db22.summary: The European Union (EU) confronts a widening productivity gap with the United States (US) and China. Informed by the Draghi Report (2024), the emerging response is a bold but narrow one, dominated by massive investment in the technologies and sectors where Europe most conspicuously lags. This article argues that pursuing parity in areas where Europe shows considerable weakness is the wrong race. The surer path runs through Europe's existing strengths —its pharmaceutical hubs, aerospace clusters, machine-tool districts and chemical bases, among others— used not as a pretext for standing still but as a springboard for reinvention. This implies mobilising the potential of every European territory by climbing the complexity ladder, absorbing new technologies into living industrial ecosystems, and diversifying into related activities that grow organically out of existing capabilities. A differentiated, place-sensitive strategy built on path dependence, brownfield digitalisation and the deliberate strengthening of European chokepoints in strategic sectors offers a more durable route to competitiveness than chasing after American or Chinese shadows. Europe is not short of talent or invention: the problem lies in institutional barriers to integration, the weakness of its knowledge-to-innovation pipeline, and its chronic inability to help promising start-ups graduate into globally significant firms. Fix those, and the case for territorial myopia collapses. For if Europe is bound to struggle at imitation, it might as well succeed at being itself and, on its own terms, lead.

4a32a2255e:72d83801ff86b493.title: The Skyscraper Revolution: Global Economic Development and Land Savings
4a32a2255e:72d83801ff86b493.author: Remi Jedwab
4a32a2255e:72d83801ff86b493.summary: Tall buildings make up over 20% of real estate by value in the world's largest cities. Nonetheless, many governments constrain tall building construction, hindering urbanization and growth. Quantification for all cities worldwide using a canonical land use model disciplined with reduced form elasticity estimates indicates that eliminating existing height constraints would generate a welfare gain of 3.7% in developing economies. Aggregate land values would decline by 3.9%, incentivizing landowners to support height restrictions. Estimated elasticities of city population and built area with respect to aggregate city building heights are 0.13 and -0.16, reinforcing the quantitative evidence that tall buildings facilitate urban growth and compactness. Interactions between static demand factors and the geography of bedrock isolate 1975-2015 tall building construction driven by technology-induced reductions in the cost of height. Using indirect inference, we estimate a (congestion) elasticity of consumer welfare to urban density of -0.11.

4a32a2255e:87b3c2b5686737f0.title: Structural Amplification in UK Production Networks between 2017 and 2022
4a32a2255e:87b3c2b5686737f0.author: Antonio Haro-Banon
4a32a2255e:87b3c2b5686737f0.summary: The UK economy experienced three major shocks between 2017 and 2022&colon Brexit, the pandemic, and the European energy crisis. This paper asks whether these events changed the structure of the UK's production network, using detailed data covering 12 UK regions and 105 industries. A key finding is that conventional measures can be misleading. On the face of it, the UK economy appeared to become more interconnected over this period, with standard input&dashoutput multipliers rising by around 5&dash6 per cent. However, once inflation and sector-specific price changes are stripped out, that increase disappears. The UK's average multiplier was essentially unchanged. The more important change was structural. Measures of how shocks propagate through supply chains show that the production network became more amplifying and more concentrated, with most of this shift occurring in 2021&dash22. The evidence points overwhelmingly to the energy sector, especially electricity and gas, as the source of this change. Brexit&dashrelated effects appear smaller, while pandemic effects are diffuse. The policy lesson is that resilience depends not only on average interconnectedness but also on where influence is concentrated. The energy&dashprice shock exposed the extent to which a small number of strategically important sectors can reshape the transmission of disturbances across the wider economy. Monitoring these structural vulnerabilities may be as important as tracking headline measures of economic activity.

33e1d7779a:9d0317701de104b9.title: Exclusive: OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio
33e1d7779a:9d0317701de104b9.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:9d0317701de104b9.summary: OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio, a startup building AI agents to help pharmaceutical companies manage drug development, the ChatGPT maker shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: Rival AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic are both pushing into science as they look to expand beyond their core competencies in coding and cybersecurity. State of play: OpenAI will integrate Orchestra's team and technology into Rosalind, its suite of AI models and tools designed for life sciences researchers, the company said. Orchestra's platform allows scientists to delegate tasks like monitoring studies, tracking drug development timelines and identifying potential delays to AI agents. Both companies aim to deploy agents that can connect scientific findings with the decisions and next steps required to advance potential treatments. Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Between the lines: AI companies don't just want to increase productivity, they want to say they are responsible for, say, curing cancer, solving math, and fundamentally changing every critical industry in the world. Those ambitions have fueled acquisitions from rival AI labs. Anthropic acquired AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio for roughly $400 million in April, according to The Information . Zoom in: OpenAI introduced its specialized GPT-Rosalind model in April to help researchers tackle complex problems in biology, chemistry and drug discovery. OpenAI has also partnered with pharmaceutical giants including Novo Nordisk and Moderna to bring AI into research and development workflows. OpenAI says developing a new medicine typically takes 10 to 15 years, a timeline it hopes AI can shorten. Zoom out Anthropic has been making its own aggressive push into life sciences. In June, Anthropic launched Claude Science , an AI-powered research platform that connects scientific databases, analysis tools and specialized agents. In September, the company announced a new biological research lab and said Claude had…

33e1d7779a:7ef07c909f9cb6d6.title: Homebuilder sentiment is at a 14-year low
33e1d7779a:7ef07c909f9cb6d6.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:7ef07c909f9cb6d6.summary: The AI boom is sucking up all the capital. The Federal Reserve is raising rates to try to cool inflation. And one sector is bearing the brunt of the pain from both: housing . The big picture: The situation is lose-lose for both homebuilders and homebuyers. Builders are facing more expensive capital and bidding for scarce construction-related resources. Would-be buyers are being quoted some of the highest mortgage rates of this century. New September housing starts data out Tuesday morning puts an exclamation point on what has been a slow-moving disaster for a sector that plays an outsized role in the economic cycle and in Americans' basic living standards. By the numbers: The number of housing units started by builders fell 5.2% last month, the Census Bureau said , to 1.22 million. It's down 7.4% year over year and near post-pandemic lows. Starts of single-family homes fell 4.6% to their lowest level since March 2023. Pending home sales fell 7.3% last month, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday morning, to the lowest since the data was tracked going back to 2001. Homebuilder sentiment fell this month to its lowest level since 2012, the National Association of Home Builders said Monday. State of play: The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was 7.4% earlier this month, Freddie Mac said in its most recent weekly reading. The rate was briefly higher than that in 2023, but has not been consistently above that level since the fall of 2000. That has kept homebuyers on the sidelines — while a parallel rise in borrowing costs for developers has made it harder for new projects to pencil out. In effect, the bottomless demand for capital from AI hyperscalers and the U.S. government has to squeeze something, and that something has been the housing sector. Residential investment has subtracted from overall GDP for five of the last six quarters. Zoom out: Housing affordability is the crux of Americans' broader dissatisfaction with economic conditions, and all…

33e1d7779a:033740f423910cf8.title: France riots become Republican midterm boogeyman
33e1d7779a:033740f423910cf8.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:033740f423910cf8.summary: As the French right-wing National Rally is seizing on fiery protests in the country for its pre-election pitch, so are President Trump and his Republican allies in the U.S. The big picture: The Trump administration has used the unrest, which began over education grievances , to bolster its messaging on immigration and the threat of "communists," a group Trump has repeatedly claimed is threatening American civilization. Driving the news: "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical 'Dumocrats' want to do to America," Trump said before a Kansas rally crowd Monday. He claimed France was being "conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity" and "the Western civilization itself." Speaking earlier to reporters, the president claimed, without evidence, that the situation in France was about "immigration, not schools." He's repeatedly blamed immigration for the protests. The White House referred Axios to the president's Truth Social post echoing that rhetoric. Catch up quick: Localized demonstrations by high school students that began in Paris last month have broadened into a massive nationwide movement over poor school conditions and costs of living, sparking thousands of arrests and clashes between police and protesters, Axios' Bec Falconer reports. The civil unrest gave way to rioting and looting, leading French President Emmanuel Macron to condemn "unrestrained violence" by "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals," per the AP . Some 550,000 people demonstrated in France Saturday, per the interior ministry, though Reuters reported that a key union estimated 800,000. On the sidelines, "thugs" chose "violence," per a translation of the interior ministry's statement , which added that some 500 police officers and firefighters were injured. The forceful police response to student demonstrators has also been scrutinized…

33e1d7779a:99a6a8bf9a88df9d.title: The manosphere stars who helped Trump win are losing their shine
33e1d7779a:99a6a8bf9a88df9d.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:99a6a8bf9a88df9d.summary: The manosphere stars who helped mobilize young men for Donald Trump in 2024 are losing their shine with that very audience. Why it matters: Trump and Republicans rode a wave of cultural cachet to reach young male voters. Now, the president and some of his most influential online allies are showing signs of losing their grip on that audience ahead of the 2026 midterms . Driving the news: New polling from the Democratic project Speaking With American Men suggests some of the most prominent influencers during Trump's 2024 campaign have lost their luster with young male voters, per Puck News , Joe Rogan's favorable rating among young men dropped from 11 points, while Elon Musk's popularity dropped 14 points and Tucker Carlson lost 12 points. Andrew Tate, who was arrested on sex trafficking and rape charges, had "a -30 net approval rating," per Puck. Between the lines: Economic pressures and the Iran war have become major concerns for young men heading into the midterms, Puck reported. Those issues have caused tension between Trump and the influential voices who bolstered his last campaign. State of play: Young men are turning on politicians, podcasters and influencers, many of whom may have influenced recent political outcomes. They're becoming more skeptical and turning their backs on politicians, especially Trump. The 2026 Young American Men Survey from Cygnal similarly found that among 18- to 30-year-old American men, Trump, Vance and the Republican Party all were viewed unfavorably. Trump's numbers among young voters dropped precipitously. Marquette Law School national polling shows that Trump's approval dropped from 40% in January 2025 to 19% in April 2026, before rebounding to 28% in June. The law school hasn't polled on the question since then. Yes, but: Young men aren't especially enthusiastic about Democrats, either. Former President Barack Obama, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), and NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani were the only Democrats showing upticks in favorability…

33e1d7779a:31e2619f9cc78072.title: How the energy crisis could become a food security crisis
33e1d7779a:31e2619f9cc78072.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:31e2619f9cc78072.summary: The Iran war and the Ukraine- Russia conflict are creating a "multidirectional squeeze on world agriculture" that could spiral into a crisis, a new report finds. Why it matters: Wars and extreme weather are colliding to threaten global food supplies and drive up prices, especially in vulnerable economies. The report explores how the El Niño phenomenon could compound the problems of restricted supplies of key fertilizer ingredients, higher fuel costs on the farm and more. The S&P Global Institute report is an unusually holistic look at the topic. Driving the news: The analysis comes alongside new warnings about food from the International Monetary Fund. Its World Economic Outlook last week sees an overall 10% increase in fertilizer prices this year and food costs rising by 5% in 2026 and 2.4% in 2027, though it depends on the region. "Higher energy and food prices could have severe effects on poverty and food security" and threaten political stability in vulnerable economies, the IMF warned. State of play: Food producers need steady supplies of natural gas and sulfur for fertilizer, diesel for farm machinery and food transport, and open sea lanes for trade, S&P notes. "Conflict is now testing all of them at once, just as El Niño tests the harvest," states the report from the research and consulting firm. "The risk is increasing, especially for low-income countries, where food costs amount to about half of household spending," it states. Zoom out: The disruptions could affect agricultural production worldwide, from soybeans and corn in Brazil to wheat in Australia, S&P finds. The intrigue: The S&P report also warns of something that has received somewhat less attention. The diesel supply crunch doesn't just raise costs for farmers. It also works alongside pro-biofuels policies to make biodiesel production more attractive. "The knock-on effect is that, in some regions, crops for fuel become more valuable than crops for food." Zoom in: A few stats via S&P illustrate…

33e1d7779a:f273d5774339218d.title: Trump isn't out to hurt Ukraine, Rubio tells Zelensky
33e1d7779a:f273d5774339218d.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:f273d5774339218d.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in a phone call Tuesday that President Trump hasn't issued any kind of order to harm Ukraine. Why it matters: The call was an effort to prevent the crisis between the U.S. and Ukraine from escalating further — and to push back on Ukrainian accusations that Trump is trying to coerce Zelensky into making concessions to Russia. The 45-minute call took place several hours ahead of a new round of peace talks with White House envoy Steve Witkoff aimed at reaching a unified position with European allies on an updated peace proposal to present to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Driving the news: The crisis broke out 10 days ago when Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia at the same time his envoys were in negotiations with Ukrainian officials in Miami. Zelensky on Monday lobbied a bipartisan group of senators to press the Trump administration to remove what he says are restrictions on intelligence sharing and weapons supplies. Behind the scenes: Rubio told reporters on Tuesday that he clarified to Zelensky that the Pentagon hasn't changed anything when it comes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine, weapons sales or restrictions on the use of the Starshield satellite system. "No change was ordered. It is not true that we restricted it," Rubio said. Rubio acknowledged to Zelensky that there could be a delay in sending Patriot interceptors that have already been paid for by NATO countries. But the reason, he said, is that the U.S. needs to make sure it has enough to protect its own military bases around the world. "Nothing is being deliberately denied. We balance between our obligations to partners and our own needs," he said. "There hasn't been a deliberate political directive to harm Ukraine." Rubio also asserted that the several cases in which Ukraine didn't get advance warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks were a result of technical failures, not a U.S. order. What he's saying: "No…

33e1d7779a:6cba97ffa33c0af6.title: AI takes on great experiment in self-rule
33e1d7779a:6cba97ffa33c0af6.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:6cba97ffa33c0af6.summary: Slowly but surely, the leading AI companies are creating a national self-governing structure to oversee their technology and its societal impact. With the federal government largely hands-off, Anthropic, OpenAI and others are self-regulating their technology and now setting up their own plans to redistribute their wealth. Why it matters: Not since the age of the robber barons have America's industrial titans wielded such sweeping power to shape society — and decide how their private fortunes should serve the public good. In the modern era, Washington has largely exercised those powers through regulation, taxation and public spending. The big picture: President Trump has no interest in new regulations. Instead, he has blessed a basic framework for the AI companies to regulate themselves — and potentially each other — outside of formal government monitoring. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Elon Musk's XSI, Meta and Nvidia are working on different versions of this. This is all voluntary and rests on the public trusting companies the size of industrialized nations to responsibly police themselves. These companies are in a frantic race to create human-surpassing superintelligence. All are pressing ahead, even as their leaders — particularly at Anthropic — warn of potentially catastrophic risks and profound economic disruption. At the same time, some AI leaders are promising to direct a portion of their vast wealth to benefit those outside their companies. Zoom in: At least three competing visions are emerging for sharing the spoils of the AI boom, each with a different answer to who should control the wealth. Anthropic: The company. On the eve of its blockbuster IPO, Anthropic pledged 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund that could grow into one of the largest philanthropic institutions in history. At a hypothetical $2 trillion valuation, its stake would be worth $100 billion — more than the Gates Foundation's current endowment. Including earlier founder and…

33e1d7779a:86a520f634a2bd62.title: Empathy divides Americans by religion, with white evangelicals standing apart
33e1d7779a:86a520f634a2bd62.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:86a520f634a2bd62.summary: Data: PRRI, 2026 American Values Survey ; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios White evangelical Protestants are the only major religious group in which a majority says empathy can become dangerous when it leads people away from a society guided by God's truth, according to a new survey . Why it matters : The survey lands amid a quiet civil war within American Christianity over who deserves empathy. Conservatives ranging from evangelical pastors to Elon Musk have framed empathy as a vulnerability in debates over immigration , racial justice and LGBTQ+ rights . In a February 2025 interview with Joe Rogan, Musk called empathy "the fundamental weakness of Western civilization," while acknowledging its potential good and warning against its weaponization. By the numbers: The annual American Values Survey from the nonpartisan Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) released Tuesday found that 42% of white evangelical Protestants agreed that empathy is a foundational moral value that helps build a healthy society. Separately, 54% agreed that empathy can become dangerous when it leads people away from a society guided by God's truth. In every other religious group, PRRI found that at least 66% agreed with the foundational-value statement, including 73% of white mainline Protestants and Hispanic Catholics. Empathy's foundational value was endorsed by 83% of religiously unaffiliated Americans, 80% of respondents grouped under other non-Christian religions, 77% of Jewish Americans and 65% of Latter-day Saints. The intrigue: The survey found a 30-point partisan gap: 84% of Democrats agreed with the foundational-value statement, compared with 54% of Republicans. Independents were at 70%. White evangelicals stand out among religious groups, but PRRI reports religious and partisan results separately. The survey doesn't establish how much white evangelicals contribute to the Republican-Democratic gap. Zoom in: The divide also tracks with PRRI's Christian nationalism measure. Among…

33e1d7779a:f2885070c43f9ddf.title: Republicans see shrinking boost from redistricting
33e1d7779a:f2885070c43f9ddf.author: Hans Nichols
33e1d7779a:f2885070c43f9ddf.summary: House Republicans are quietly scaling back hopes for the 10-seat boost they sought from redistricting nationwide, amid a souring political climate and polls showing a collapse in GOP support among Latino voters in Texas and Florida . Why it matters: On their down days, Republicans privately worry that the great redistricting war of 2026 will net them only one seat nationwide, according to top GOP strategists. Zoom out: At the beginning of the cycle, Republicans viewed redistricting like an umbrella in a storm: It could keep their House majority dry in a light drizzle — but in a political hurricane, it wouldn't be enough. They're not second-guessing the redistricting strategy, even as they wince at the price tag. According to AdImpact, Republicans have spent $133 million on TV ads trying to win in 15 redrawn districts that were supposed to be easy pickings. Still, they no longer talk seriously about redistricting saving their House majority, as they did a year ago — before the Iran war helped boost inflation and sink President Trump's approval ratings. By the numbers: Early this summer, Republicans believed they had created 16 more GOP-friendly seats: five in Texas , four in Florida , two in Ohio and one each in Alabama , Louisiana , Missouri , North Carolina and Tennessee . But since then, courts tossed a Missouri map and the political environment has darkened, with Democrats holding an 8-percentage-point lead in new Washington Post-ABC polling . GOP support has eroded particularly among Latino voters , raising Republican fears of losing seats their mapmakers counted on after Trump nearly won the Hispanic vote outright in 2024. "Texas, I'd be surprised if we got all five," Rep. Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios this month. "Florida, I'd be shocked if we got all four." The other side: Then factor in California , where Gov. Gavin Newsom, eager to show his party he was willing to fight back, engineered a new map with four more solidly Democratic seats — and one slightly…

33e1d7779a:20704f9eec503ad8.title: The budget deficit swells, while the cost of debt rises
33e1d7779a:20704f9eec503ad8.author: Emily Peck
33e1d7779a:20704f9eec503ad8.summary: Data: Office of Management and Budget via Fred , U.S. Treasury; Note: 2026 GDP estimated using extrapolated Q3 growth via CFRB; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios The U.S. budget deficit is ballooning, reaching $2 trillion this fiscal year, according to the latest figures. Why it matters: That's the largest deficit since 2021, when the U.S. was climbing out of the pandemic recession. The deficit is being driven in part by the cost of servicing the nation's enormous debt at a time when interest rates are rising due, in part, to the inflationary impact of the Iran war. By the numbers: The federal government paid out $1.052 trillion in net interest on its outstanding debt — all those Treasury notes and bonds we keep writing about — for the 2026 fiscal year, which ended Sept. 30, according to the Treasury data. That's more than what was spent on defense, and was the country's third-biggest outlay after Social Security ($1.67 trillion) and Medicare ($1.07 trillion). Stunning stat: Federal net interest costs in 2026 are estimated at 3.3% of GDP, which would be a record high, according to an estimate from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. Between the lines: This is the price tag for years of borrowing at much higher interest rates — a sort of new normal since inflation started rising in 2021. Rising interest costs add to the deficit, driving still more borrowing and putting additional pressure on the federal budget. The intrigue: The last time interest costs approached these levels was when President George H.W. Bush was in office. At the time, the administration negotiated a bipartisan deficit reduction package that raised taxes, breaking President Bush's infamous "Read my lips, no new taxes" pledge and arguably led to him losing re-election. Still, in the 1990s, the Clinton administration and Congress worked to balance the budget through tax increases and spending cuts. What to watch: There's little appetite for that kind of work from either party, but the so-called…

33e1d7779a:99fe5837d6426a1d.title: "Power is probably the forever bottleneck": Grid delays threaten the AI race.
33e1d7779a:99fe5837d6426a1d.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:99fe5837d6426a1d.summary: Silicon Valley moves fast and breaks things, but the U.S. electrical grid moves slowly and requires permits. The explosive growth of AI is colliding with the glacial pace of building out new power infrastructure, prompting a new warning from Goldman Sachs that energy bottlenecks are set to stall the AI race. Why it matters : Amid a wave of anxiety from Wall Street about the debt-fueled AI buildout, Goldman points to power as the biggest risk to trillions in spending in a new report shared exclusively with Axios. Driving the news: Goldman expects global data center power demand to surge 170% between 2025 and 2030, with more than 60% of that growth coming from the U.S., according to the report . "Power is probably the forever bottleneck," Jason Tofsky, Goldman's global head of digital infrastructure investment banking, noted in the report. The bank estimates roughly $7.6 trillion in capital spending between 2026 and 2031 across computing, data centers and power infrastructure. Zoom in: The physical infrastructure needed to support AI is moving far more slowly than the technology itself. The U.S. has roughly 2,600 gigawatts of proposed power generation and storage projects awaiting grid connections, more than twice the grid's existing installed capacity, though many projects may never materialize. The median time from an application for a grid connection to commercial operation is roughly five years. Between the lines: The so-called AI race, which has long been defined by advances in frontier AI models, is really about who can get their hands on enough power, Goldman argues. That could mean a longer, less predictable buildout, delayed financial returns and greater risks for companies investing heavily before securing power. Follow the money: The massive expansion is being financed with debt, raising the stakes if construction timelines slip. Goldman projects $420 billion in global hyperscaler debt issuance in 2027, up more than 60% from its 2026 estimate. Debt is…

33e1d7779a:df7a2b02644ca40e.title: I let agents plan a WNBA Finals trip (but kept my wallet to myself)
33e1d7779a:df7a2b02644ca40e.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:df7a2b02644ca40e.summary: Let's call it the Battle of the Bots, part 1: I decided to put two of the newest personal AI agents, OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse , through their paces, with the WNBA Finals providing a natural testing ground. Why it matters: AI companies are racing to create the digital assistant we turn to for everything from shopping to travel planning. But there's still a gap between what these agents can do and what I'm comfortable letting them do. They also need to pass what we'll call "The Human Benchmark" : that is, can they do something as fast, or as well, as a human? The answer is ... not quite yet, but the capabilities are still impressive. The big picture: For the test, I asked each assistant to plan a fantasy trip to Atlanta to see my beloved Golden State Valkyries, organize a purple-themed brunch watch party and create souvenir programs. I also had them help me shop for Valkyries merch, which eventually turned into a side quest for WNBA basketball cards. The cost: Muse is free for most uses, with optional $20 and $100 monthly subscriptions. Dots requires a ChatGPT Pro subscription, starting at $100 monthly, or access through a business or enterprise plan. More on Dots . Where they shined: Both agents were surprisingly good at handling complicated, multistep assignments. When I asked them to find flights and tickets for Game 3 in Atlanta, both caught that the game had been moved up a day and that tickets weren't yet on sale to the general public. The available seats were being offered through the resale market, likely at inflated prices. Both found good flight options. Muse opened a browser and let me enter my information to try to sign up for a ticket presale. Dots, meanwhile, flagged a scheduling conflict with an enrollment fair, which it gleaned from my AI-assisted effort to keep tabs on the joys of finding the right high school in San Francisco. Where they were creative, but imperfect: Both agents could turn broad instructions into surprisingly elaborate…

33e1d7779a:ffac654a1bc9fdac.title: Witkoff heads to Oslo, plans Russia trip for peace talks
33e1d7779a:ffac654a1bc9fdac.author: Rebecca Falconer
33e1d7779a:ffac654a1bc9fdac.summary: White House envoy Steve Witkoff is traveling to Oslo for talks Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders, a U.S. official said. The big picture: The talks will bring together Ukraine, European allies and the U.S. as they seek to develop a peace proposal to present to Russia . The Oslo talks are expected to include Zelensky , Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, representatives of the E4 nations (the U.K., France, Germany and Poland) and officials from the EU and NATO. Driving the news: The U.S. official said that following Oslo, Witkoff is also planning to travel to Russia, where he hopes to meet with President Vladimir Putin and present ideas developed in close consultation with Ukraine and European partners. Trump adviser Jared Kushner has the flu and will not attend the Oslo meeting in person, but will participate virtually, the U.S. official said. The planned meetings in Oslo build on the discussions held at Witkoff's Miami-area Shell Bay club , where Zelensky committed to reviewing and advancing a series of proposals aimed at creating a pathway toward a comprehensive and durable peace agreement, the U.S. official added. Zoom in: The U.S. official said American, Ukrainian and European representatives worked together over the past week to develop the proposals. "Steve and Jared also spoke with President Zelensky on Sunday to review progress and discuss next steps," the U.S. official said. The trip is also expected to include efforts to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher whom the U.S. says has been wrongfully detained in Russia. What's next: The U.S. official said the discussions are focused on two parallel tracks: Securing Ukraine's future: Establishing a sovereign, secure, and prosperous future for Ukraine, including credible security guarantees, European integration, and a comprehensive postwar economic framework that addresses Ukraine's financial needs and creates opportunities for long-term…

33e1d7779a:dc29d45a22397f89.title: Scoop: Pete Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections
33e1d7779a:dc29d45a22397f89.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:dc29d45a22397f89.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel on Monday, two sources with knowledge told Axios. Why it matters: The unannounced visit comes eight days before Israel's election and amid U.S.-Israeli discussions about potentially resuming major combat operations against Iran . Driving the news: The meeting with Netanyahu took place at Ovda Air Base in southern Israel, where U.S. refueling planes and fighter jets are deployed, two sources said. The Pentagon and the Israeli Embassy declined to comment. The Israeli Prime Minister's office didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story. Please check back for updates.
