57a95411f6:b6481603652e7c6f.title: Habeas Class Actions
57a95411f6:b6481603652e7c6f.author: Mira Yu
57a95411f6:b6481603652e7c6f.summary: Can habeas corpus cases proceed as class actions? The Supreme Court has never squarely answered that question, even in cases where lower courts certified habeas classes. But the Trump Administration’s wholesale push to expel noncitizens has forced the question to the center of modern civil rights litigation. The post Habeas Class Actions appeared first on Harvard Law Review .

57a95411f6:e3ab75c32d22fab3.title: Indigenous Constitutionalism
57a95411f6:e3ab75c32d22fab3.author: Mira Yu
57a95411f6:e3ab75c32d22fab3.summary: By standard accounts, there are fifty-four constitutions across the federal, state, and territorial governments of the United States. But in fact, there are 230 other governmental constitutions that currently govern peoples and territories within the United States. These constitutions not only flow from a sovereignty that existed prior to the United States but also came out of a legal movement that asserted its independence from both the U.S. Constitution and state constitutions. This Article tells the story of these constitutions — the constitutions of Native nations. The post Indigenous Constitutionalism appeared first on Harvard Law Review .

57a95411f6:f5a891d07c8cfd7f.title: What is a Tort?
57a95411f6:f5a891d07c8cfd7f.author: Mira Yu
57a95411f6:f5a891d07c8cfd7f.summary: What is a tort, and what is tort law for? On one leading scholarly account, torts are legal liability rules that seek to promote the welfare of society at large by disincentivizing socially suboptimal behavior and distributing the costs of accidents to those who can best bear them. The post What is a Tort? appeared first on Harvard Law Review .

57a95411f6:816fb4de05c05581.title: Drug Scheduling as Institutional Design
57a95411f6:816fb4de05c05581.author: Mira Yu
57a95411f6:816fb4de05c05581.summary: The United States makes bad choices when it comes to psychoactive drugs. Under the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), U.S. drug law has simultaneously fueled mass incarceration, inhibited needed access, and enabled an opioid crisis. The post Drug Scheduling as Institutional Design appeared first on Harvard Law Review .

57a95411f6:87086dc691de88ad.title: Practical Consequences in Statutory Interpretation
57a95411f6:87086dc691de88ad.author: Mira Yu
57a95411f6:87086dc691de88ad.summary: Modern textualism has long criticized the use of practical, or consequentialist, reasoning when construing statutes. And yet in practice, textualist jurists long have invoked practical consequences arguments to help justify their statutory constructions. The post Practical Consequences in Statutory Interpretation appeared first on Harvard Law Review .

b0b006b3d4:3f7e1a446afda47e.title: Combating the Whirlwind with a Single Sheet of Paper
b0b006b3d4:3f7e1a446afda47e.author: Cal Newport
b0b006b3d4:3f7e1a446afda47e.summary: One of the more debilitating experiences in our current digital world is the sense of being trapped in relentless, reactive, busyness. This “whirlwind” can separate you from both ambition and presence, leaving you feeling flat and fried. In this episode, Cal discusses a simple trick he deploys when he finds himself in this state. It requires only a single sheet of paper. Knowledge Spillovers, Competition, and Individual Careers Thomas Cornelissen, Christian Dustmann, Uta Schönberg American Economic Review Workplace peers can affect early careers through both knowledge spillovers and competition for promotion. Using untrained labor-market entrants and variation in whether coworkers share an occupation, the analysis finds persistent positive spillovers alongside competition effects of similar size; both are stronger for men. Racial Promotion Gaps Deepak Hegde, Alexander Ljungqvist, Manav Raj American Economic Review Promotion delays at the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office create substantial racial disparities even under formulaic rules. Administrative records show that Black patent examiners reach entitled promotions about a year later and lose 2.5% of career earnings; the pattern is inconsistent with accurate statistical discrimination or supervisor taste and instead fits belief-based discrimination. Social Push and the Direction of Innovation Elias Einiö, Josh Feng, Xavier Jaravel American Economic Review Linked U.S. and Finnish data show that inventors disproportionately create products purchased by people similar to themselves in gender, age, and socioeconomic status. Embedding this social matching in a growth model indicates that unequal access to innovation careers meaningfully shapes both the cost-of-living distribution and long-run growth. Monetary Policy Invariance, Hysteresis, and Optimal Inflation Mirko Abbritti, Agostino Consolo, Sebastian Weber Review of Economic Studies A New Keynesian model with endogenous productivity and downward nominal-wage rigidity links unemployment fluctuations to R&D and hysteresis. The resulting long-run Phillips curve is nonvertical, and balancing price distortions against output losses raises the welfare-maximizing inflation target above 2%; unemployment-responsive Taylor rules better contain the asymmetry. Firm Heterogeneity, Market Power, and Macroeconomic Fragility Alessandro Ferrari, Francisco Queirós American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics How do firm heterogeneity and market power affect the risk of prolonged macroeconomic slumps? A calibrated quantitative model incorporates trends in dispersion across firms and studies feedback among entry, competition, and factor supply. Greater heterogeneity and market power raise both the probability and expected duration of slow recoveries. The model attributes this fragility to self-reinforcing interactions that can generate multiple steady states. Do Workfare Programs Live Up to Their Promises? Experimental Evidence from Côte d'Ivoire Marianne Bertrand, Bruno Crépon, Alicia Marguerie, Patrick Premand American Economic Journal: Applied Economics Using machine learning to analyze heterogeneity, shows that alternative targeting approaches can substantially improve welfare. (JEL C45, G51, H53, I38, J13, J64, O15) During the program, the employment rate only increases slightly, but finds a shift toward wage jobs, higher earnings and savings, as well as positive changes in work habits, behaviors, and well-being. After the program, finds no lasting impact on employment or behaviors, with only limited gains in earnings stemming from independent activities. Innovation through Inventor Mobility: Evidence from Noncompete Agreements Kate Reinmuth, Emma Rockall American Economic Journal: Applied Economics Do noncompete agreements increase innovation by strengthening firms' incentives to invest in ideas? Entry and Profits in an Aging Economy: The Role of Consumer Inertia Gideon Bornstein Review of Economic Studies Can population aging explain declining business entry and rising profits? A calibrated firm-dynamics model combines overlapping consumer generations with household evidence that older consumers switch products less readily. Greater inertia makes entry harder and permits incumbents to raise markups. The model attributes 20–30% of the decline in young firms and rise in profits to aging, with state and product-category comparisons supporting its predictions. How to craft a mission? A Theory of Action for the strategic public management of mission-oriented innovation policy Iacopo Gronchi Research Policy What must public managers do to make innovation missions work? A qualitative synthesis develops a theory of implementation and illustrates it with DARPA, China's new-energy-vehicle program, and European smart specialization. Three roles recur: enabling strategic learning, maintaining adaptive accountability across project portfolios, and coordinating innovation among participating actors. Mission success depends on how managers perform these roles within their institutional constraints. Path dependence and path breaking in the fourth industrial revolution: digital technological diversification in Chinese firms Xiaodan Yu, Dan Luo, Simone Maria Grabner, Qingzhi Zhang Industrial and Corporate Change How do firms in catching-up economies develop digital inventive capabilities? Patents from Chinese listed firms during 2000–2020 show strong dependence on prior capabilities, particularly in enabling technologies. Internal innovation efforts and ownership have limited influence on breaking these paths. In application domains, firms combining research alliances with connections to public science are better able to diversify beyond established capabilities. Screening Property Rights for Innovation William Matcham, Mark Schankerman Econometrica How effectively does patent examination screen property rights, and can its costs be reduced? A dynamic structural model combines examiner incentives, intrinsic motivation, and repeated negotiation, estimated using examiner decisions and a text-based measure of patent distance. Screening is moderately effective under current patentability standards, with examiner motivation substantially improving quality. Estimated annual social costs are $15.38 billion, about 5% of U.S. private R&D; limiting negotiation rounds substantially reduces those costs. Security Design Under Common‐Value Competition Yue Yuan Econometrica Why do investors competing to finance an entrepreneur offer debt? A security-design model gives bidders dispersed information about a common-value project and allows the entrepreneur to learn from their offers. Debt limits exposure to the winner's curse with two bidders, while an informed entrepreneur is more likely to select debt when optimistic about the project. These forces outweigh signaling through the security choice, and committing to an ordered menu of securities does not raise the entrepreneur's revenue. Adoption survival frontiers: Artificial intelligence, financing frictions, and market structure Dávid Zoltán Szabó, Péter Juhász Research Policy Why might smaller firms abandon AI adoption even when the technology would be profitable? Equity Frictions and Firm Ownership Alessandra Peter Review of Economic Studies How much do equity-market frictions constrain entrepreneurship? Firm ownership and financing data across Eurozone countries discipline a general-equilibrium model of workers and entrepreneurs choosing debt and equity. Harmonizing equity frictions produces nearly four times the output effect of harmonizing debt frictions; eliminating them produces a 73% larger effect. Equity's greater risk sharing encourages expansion and accounts for over 70% of the model-explained variation in top wealth shares. On sci-tech paradigms: an essay on the economics of innovation Nicola De Liso Industrial and Corporate Change When does innovation policy need to treat science and technology as a joint activity? A conceptual analysis revisits scientific and technological paradigms and the economic incentives connecting them. In some important settings, their convergence creates a combined sci-tech paradigm that cannot be separated meaningfully into discovery and application. The implication is that policy indicators built around their independence can mischaracterize innovation opportunities. Product and process innovation and R&D spending show little response, while firm growth and native employment increase. bdf3a6bcc5:57ef2a6dc6f44d2f.title: Private Equity Ownership and Firm Performance: A Framework for Interpreting the Evidence
bdf3a6bcc5:57ef2a6dc6f44d2f.author: Per Strömberg and Christian Thomann
bdf3a6bcc5:57ef2a6dc6f44d2f.summary: We review the evidence on the impact of private equity (PE) ownership on firms, stakeholders, and the economy. We organize this literature using a framework that emphasizes the costs and benefits of PE as an ownership form and implies five main predictions: ( a ) Only some firms are natural PE targets, ( b ) PE ownership is optimally temporary, ( c ) debt is typically a cheaper source of capital than PE equity, ( d ) PE activity is strongly cyclical, and ( e ) the PE model is a second-best response to underlying agency and contracting frictions. We use this framework to interpret existing evidence and to clarify when, and for whom, PE ownership creates value.

bdf3a6bcc5:65ae2894f3cbc19f.title: Networks in Finance: Foundations and Frontiers
bdf3a6bcc5:65ae2894f3cbc19f.author: Michael Gofman, Bernard Herskovic and Gill Segal
bdf3a6bcc5:65ae2894f3cbc19f.summary: Networks in finance shape how value is created and how risks emerge, both systemic and systematic. We survey how different networks, including production, banking, director, and information networks, propagate micro shocks and transmit them to broader levels of aggregation. First, we synthesize the literature on the efficiency–stability trade-off governing systemic risk: Interconnections transmit gains, liquidity, and knowledge but create channels for contagion. Beyond the foundational focus on within-network transmission, we extend the discussion to across-network spillovers. Second, moving from systemic to systematic risk, we show how network topology drives the stochastic discount factor, affecting factors and expected returns. We also trace how networks form and evolve, dynamically generating new sources of risk. By adopting a macro perspective that unifies distinct networks into an overarching network of networks (meta-network), we focus on shared propagation mechanisms and outline directions for future research, including how networks may evolve with the rise of AI, intangibles, and deglobalization.

bdf3a6bcc5:7b98cebf159aedf4.title: The Evolution of the Corporate Bond Market: A Theoretical Analysis
bdf3a6bcc5:7b98cebf159aedf4.author: Mahyar Kargar, Benjamin Lester, Semih Üslü and Pierre-Olivier Weill
bdf3a6bcc5:7b98cebf159aedf4.summary: We develop a model of a dealer-intermediated over-the-counter market designed to study three major changes in the structure of the US corporate bond market: the increase in dealers’ balance sheet costs, the emergence of electronic trading platforms, and the growing presence of bond mutual funds and exchange-traded funds. Our model provides a unified analysis of these changes, clarifies the economic channels at play, and allows us to quantify their effects on a variety of market outcomes. Our quantitative analysis suggests that while electronic trading significantly reduced the cost of raising capital in the corporate bond market, these gains were almost completely offset by the combined effects of balance sheet costs and changes in the demand for liquidity. We find that electronic trading also caused a meaningful decline in the bid-ask spread, whereas other changes in the market structure had little effect on transaction costs.

bdf3a6bcc5:5f3eb76490d35d0a.title: Interest Rate Risk, Bank Stability, and Valuation
bdf3a6bcc5:5f3eb76490d35d0a.author: Erica Jiang, Gregor Matvos, Tomasz Piskorski and Amit Seru
bdf3a6bcc5:5f3eb76490d35d0a.summary: This article surveys recent theoretical and empirical advancements on the impact of interest rates on bank valuations and stability—two crucial concerns for financial researchers, policy makers, and regulators. We begin by highlighting the distinctive feature of the regional banking crisis of 2023—the prevalence of liquid assets on bank balance sheets—in contrast to earlier crises such as the savings and loan crisis of the 1980s and 1990s, where illiquid assets contributed to banking failure. In Section 2, we present a theoretical framework that integrates both asset illiquidity and the risk of self-fulfilling solvency runs on the deposit franchise. We show the conditions under which the deposit franchise fails to hedge asset declines due to rising interest rates and demonstrate how and why this amplifies bank fragility. Sections 3–5 explore empirical methods for assessing these effects. We review approaches to measuring the interest rate sensitivity of bank asset values, highlighting their limitations. We also examine recent advances in quantifying bank fragility, particularly the challenges of valuing the deposit franchise under both stable conditions and crisis scenarios. Additionally, we discuss new measures of bank fragility that capture the potential endogenous collapse of franchise value during crises. Applying these measures leads us to conclude that US banks face significant unhedged interest rate exposure in their asset portfolios. When combined with their high leverage, this exposure substantially increases the risk of solvency runs. Liquidity interventions, while useful in the short term, are insufficient for addressing the systemic risks posed by this vulnerability.

dc749d5ffb:a91d5080492456b7.title: Dynamic Contracting
dc749d5ffb:a91d5080492456b7.author: Alessandro Pavan
dc749d5ffb:a91d5080492456b7.summary: Dynamic contracting plays a central role in many environments—for instance, in the sale of goods and services to consumers whose preferences evolve through learning, experimentation, or habit formation; in the taxation of workers whose productivity changes with learning-by-doing; in the provision of services on platforms with stochastic entry and exit of buyers and sellers; and in the matching of agents whose values and attractiveness are gradually revealed through past interactions. This article surveys several strands of the recent dynamic mechanism design literature, distills a few lessons, and points to promising directions for future research.

dc749d5ffb:22adaf9523ee9034.title: The Economics of Professional Decision-Making: Can Artificial Intelligence Reduce Decision Uncertainty?
dc749d5ffb:22adaf9523ee9034.author: W. Bentley MacLeod
dc749d5ffb:22adaf9523ee9034.summary: This article outlines an economic model that provides a framework for organizing the growing literature on the performance of physicians and judges. The primary task of these professionals is to make decisions based on the information provided by their clients. The article discusses professional decisions in terms of what Kahneman (2011) calls fast and slow decisions, known as System 1 and System 2 in cognitive science. Slow decisions correspond to the economist's model of rational choice, while System 1 (fast) decisions are high-speed, intuitive choices guided by training and human capital. This distinction is used to provide a model of decision-making under uncertainty based on Bewley’s (2011) theory of Knightian uncertainty to show that human values are an essential input to optimal choice. This, in turn, provides conditions under which artificial intelligence (AI) tools can assist professional decision-making, while pointing to cases in which such tools need to explicitly incorporate human values in order to make better decisions.

dc749d5ffb:6c3a05b1482f2389.title: The Governance Triangle: Economic Interactions in Civil Society, the State, and the Market
dc749d5ffb:6c3a05b1482f2389.author: Samuel Bowles and Wendy Carlin
dc749d5ffb:6c3a05b1482f2389.summary: Interactions in civil society are personal and enduring, and as a result, identity and other-regarding preferences are important motivations. Here we add civil society to markets and states as a third form of governance of the economy, creating the governance triangle. We provide evidence that themes related to civil society have assumed substantially greater importance in economic research since the 1970s. A now-standard principal–agent model of employment in private firms reveals three characteristics of interactions in civil society: the importance of face-to-face interactions, social norms, and the private exercise of power. We show that market failures and other coordination problems can sometimes be more successfully addressed by civil society than by state or market governance. Civil society may have a comparative institutional advantage where conflicts of interest are modest and information available to state and market actors is limited. When based on us-versus-them forms of identity, however, civil society governance may promote preferences antithetical to a liberal and democratic society.

dc749d5ffb:1b0388d560259522.title: Evidence in Games and Mechanisms
dc749d5ffb:1b0388d560259522.author: Elchanan Ben-Porath, Eddie Dekel and Barton L. Lipman
dc749d5ffb:1b0388d560259522.summary: We survey theoretical work on the use of evidence, including work in game theory and in mechanism design.

dc749d5ffb:289d26111ffd5a84.title: Natural Language Processing and Innovation Research
dc749d5ffb:289d26111ffd5a84.author: Antonin Bergeaud, Adam Jaffe and Dimitris Papanikolaou
dc749d5ffb:289d26111ffd5a84.summary: Innovation is central to models in economics, strategy, management, and finance, yet it remains difficult to measure due to its intangible and knowledge-based nature. Recent advancements in natural language processing offer new methods to analyze textual artifacts, providing empirical insights into previously hard-to-measure aspects of innovation. This article provides an overview of the current applications of these methods in empirical innovation research, highlights their transformative potential for reshaping how researchers study and quantify innovation, and discusses the critical challenges that accompany their use.
